location.exact_line: An investigator uses a fair coin to select one channel and receives a positive report. She knows the model just described. The report's probability is 0.9 if H is true: a sound channel certainly reports positively, while a randomizing channel does so half the time. Its probability is 0.1 if H is false. The investigator's rational confidence in H is therefore 0.9.

Crucially, it is 0.9 whether A or B was selected. The channels have identical initial credentials. After observing the positive report, learning which one supplied it would make no difference to her confidence in H. Suppose she already knows which one she used. She now proposes to retain the positive report and the model, including her justified confidence, but delete the channel's identity. There is no distortion of her present assessment. She is not suppressing an objection, forgetting that she reasoned badly, or inflating a probability by omitting an unfavorable result.

explicit_printed_premises.exact_line: Consider two channels, A and B, each reporting on whether a proposition H is true. Initially H and its negation are equally probable. Each channel has an independent probability of 0.8 of being sound. A sound channel reports H's truth value perfectly. An unsound channel produces a fair random answer, independently of H. Which channels are sound is also independent of H.

An investigator uses a fair coin to select one channel and receives a positive report. She knows the model just described. The report's probability is 0.9 if H is true: a sound channel certainly reports positively, while a randomizing channel does so half the time. Its probability is 0.1 if H is false. The investigator's rational confidence in H is therefore 0.9.

location.exact_line: Tomorrow a routine audit will disclose which channels were sound. Imagine its finding is that A randomized while B was sound. If the investigator used A, her positive report now gives her no reason to prefer H to its negation: her posterior is 0.5. If she used B, her posterior is 1 in this idealized model. A retained identity would tell her which response is appropriate.

Without the identity, she must average the possibilities. Conditional on the audit and the positive report, each channel remains equally likely to have been selected. Her confidence is now 0.75. That is the appropriate assessment given what survives. But it is a poorer epistemic position than the one she could cheaply have preserved. She has lost the ability to distinguish a report whose force has collapsed from one whose force has increased.

location.exact_line: The original report helps locate the issue. Judges received a hypothetical sexual-assault case, with or without additional sexual-history information. Exposed judges first ruled on its admissibility; all then answered a guilt question requiring reliance only on admitted evidence. The conviction counts were 27/55 without exposure, 7/35 among those ruling the information inadmissible, and 1/13 among those admitting it: the reported 49.1%, 20%, and 7.7%. The last two groups were formed by the judges' own rulings, and their difference was not statistically significant (Fisher's exact p = .42). The researchers also note that judges admitting the information may have regarded it as more probative. [Wistrich, Guthrie and Rachlinski 2005, pp.1283–84, 1300–03, 1336–37](https://repository.law.upenn.edu/Documents/Detail/can-judges-ignore-inadmissible-information-the-difficulty-of-deliberately-disregarding/153906)

location.exact_line: Imagine a population of judges. Each has a baseline deliberative score, x, representing how strongly the admissible case supports conviction relative to the judge's threshold. A positive final score produces conviction; a negative score produces acquittal. Let baseline scores be uniformly distributed from −0.509 to 0.491. The interval has length one, and its positive part has length 0.491. Without the extra consideration, 49.1% therefore convict.

When counted at full strength, suppose the extra consideration subtracts 0.414 from each judge's score. A judge then convicts only if x exceeds 0.414. The relevant portion of the interval has length 0.077, producing the second rate of 7.7%.

In the second model, every judge responds to the rule by reducing the weight assigned to the consideration, but nobody eliminates that weight. Each now subtracts 0.291 rather than 0.414. Each still treats the information as counting against conviction. A judge convicts when x exceeds 0.291. The relevant portion of the interval has length 0.200. Again, exactly 20% convict.

explicit_printed_premises.exact_line: Imagine a population of judges. Each has a baseline deliberative score, x, representing how strongly the admissible case supports conviction relative to the judge's threshold. A positive final score produces conviction; a negative score produces acquittal. Let baseline scores be uniformly distributed from −0.509 to 0.491. The interval has length one, and its positive part has length 0.491. Without the extra consideration, 49.1% therefore convict.

In the first model, some judges completely exclude the consideration because they accept the rule as a reason not to rely on it. They recognize its apparent force, but remove it from the basis of their decision. The rest continue to count it at full strength. Let the proportion of complete excluders be q, independently of their baseline scores. The overall conviction rate is then:
